name: Beard growth serum / Kirkland minox foam

card.summary: Over-the-counter 5% minoxidil foam, often a store-brand like Kirkland, used off-label on the beard; the only active ingredient with trial evidence for beard growth.
card.aka: Kirkland minoxidil foam, Rogaine foam, beard serum
card.note: Off-label for beard use; effects reportedly reverse when stopped; beard "serums" vary in ingredients.

quick.overview:
Minoxidil is an over-the-counter topical sold for scalp hair loss, and 5% foam products, including store brands, are widely discussed for beard growth. Commercial beard "serums" are a separate and varied category.

Small randomized trials of minoxidil lotion for beard enhancement exist, and Wikipedia lists beard growth as an off-label use.
quick.mechanism: Minoxidil is a prodrug converted in follicles to minoxidil sulfate, an ATP-sensitive potassium channel opener; proposed hair effects include increased blood flow and growth-factor induction.
quick.risks: Topical use can cause itching, irritation and dandruff; hypertrichosis (unwanted hair growth) is described, and benefits reverse when use stops.

lead: Minoxidil topical foam and solution are sold over the counter in the US for androgenetic alopecia, with 5% foam approved in 2006 and generics following in 2017.[1] Beard growth is described as an off-label use, and trials have been published in transgender men and in beard enhancement generally.[1][3]
Commercial beard growth serums are marketed under many brand names; the contents differ by product, and no studies found address them as a class.

paras: Minoxidil is a prodrug whose active metabolite, minoxidil sulfate, is formed mainly by SULT1A1 in follicles.[1] Topical absorption is only about 1.2 to 1.4 percent.[1]
Topical use can cause itching, irritation, dandruff and unwanted hair growth elsewhere on the body.[1] Hair benefits require continued use, and effects reverse after discontinuation.[1]
Upjohn developed the compound in the late 1950s; topical minoxidil was approved as Rogaine in 1988 and became OTC in 1996.[1]

A randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled study of 3% minoxidil lotion for beard enhancement was published in the Journal of Dermatology in 2016, and a randomized trial of 3% topical minoxidil for facial hair enhancement in transgender men was published in 2026.[3] Wikipedia also lists beard growth, including studies in transgender men, as an off-label use.[1]

timeline.event: Topical minoxidil (Rogaine) approved for male baldness.[1]
